title: How We’re Learning to Talk to Animals
summary: Josh and Chuck explore research into decoding and possibly speaking animal languages, reversing the usual approach of teaching animals human language. Topics include pets and facial expressions (dog eyebrow muscle, adoption rates), horse-human communication, honeyguide birds and the Jahua and Hadza people, bird song recording and the Merlin app, early primate alarm-call research (vervet monkeys, Campbell's monkeys and suffixes), prairie dog vocal language, Japanese tit word order experiments, honeybee waggle dance, dialects in great apes and naked mole rats, Roger Payne's humpback whale album and Save the Whales movement, sperm whale clan codas, orca and dolphin vocal learning and signature whistles, spindle cells and empathy, AI-driven animal translation projects (Project CETI, Earth Species Project), and a listener mail segment.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Hosts joke about dolphin sounds and introduce the episode on research into understanding and possibly speaking animal languages, distinct from teaching animals human language.

segments.title: Pets, dogs and Descartes
segments.summary: Discussion of science long denying animal inner lives, Descartes' influence, and dog facial expressions such as the eyebrow muscle that helped dogs get adopted faster, plus MRI studies of dogs' brains.

segments.title: Horses and human communication
segments.summary: Horse trainer and neuroscientist Janet Jones's view that horses and humans communicate through body cues, with horses' wide visual range and prey origins; riders become a kind of super organism.

segments.title: Honeyguide birds and human calls
segments.summary: Jahua people in Mozambique and Hadza people in Tanzania use calls to attract honeyguide birds, which lead them to honey in a mutually beneficial relationship; the calls are passed down through generations.

segments.title: Bird song and recording
segments.summary: History of notating bird song and modern collections at Cornell, plus the Merlin bird identification app.

segments.title: Seventies research on primate alarm calls
segments.summary: Seyfarth, Cheney and Marler found vervet monkeys in Kenya use different calls for eagles and snakes, prompting recognition that animal calls may carry meaning.

segments.title: Campbell's monkey suffixes and cross-species learning
segments.summary: Zuberbühler found Campbell's monkeys in Côte d'Ivoire combine alarm calls with suffixes that change meaning; other species nearby learn these calls, and Chuck compares it to pet food cues.

segments.title: Prairie dog vocal language
segments.summary: Slobodchikoff's research on prairie dogs: distinct sounds describe predator type, size, color and speed, can combine them to describe new threats, and have a tonal language; they describe humans by features.

segments.title: Japanese tits, honeybees and learned versus innate communication
segments.summary: Japanese tits respond to word order of snake calls, showing grammar. Honeybee waggle dance is partly innate and partly learned, per a 2023 study; Carl von Frisch decoded it with a Nobel Prize in 1973.

segments.title: Great ape gestures, dialects and naked mole rats
segments.summary: Great apes share similar gestures with regional variation, comparable to dialects; naked mole rats respond to colony-specific chirps. The come-here gesture may be ancient.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the whale section.

segments.title: Roger Payne and humpback whale songs
segments.summary: Navy listening station recordings of whale song reached scientists, and Roger Payne's 1970 album Songs of the Humpback Whale helped fuel the Save the Whales movement. Chuck and Josh differ on listening to it.

segments.title: Sperm whale clan codas and loudness
segments.summary: Sperm whale clans use distinct coda click patterns as identifiers, with clicks around 236 decibels. Josh's Don't Be Dumb reference.

segments.title: Orca and dolphin vocal learning
segments.summary: Orcas babble as calves and learn vocalizations until puberty; orcas eavesdrop on dolphins; bottlenose dolphins create individual signature whistles as names.

segments.title: Brain spindle cells and empathy
segments.summary: Spindle cells in the anterior cingulate cortex and frontal insula support self-monitoring and empathy; sperm whales have more of them than humans, and great apes and other cetaceans also have them.

segments.title: Crows and AI as a translation tool
segments.summary: Crows have complex vocalizations beyond human listening ability; AI language models are being used to detect patterns in animal sounds, starting with Deep Squeak for rodents.

segments.title: Project CETI and Earth Species Project
segments.summary: Project CETI listens to a sperm whale clan off Dominica with robotic fish and needs millions of recordings; Earth Species Project aims to map species languages and speak to animals. Hosts discuss implications for humanity and meat eating.

segments.title: Whale conversation hopes and AI risks
segments.summary: Discussion of what humans and whales could talk about, shared concepts like grief and joy, and the risk that AI-whale conversations could be unintelligible.

segments.title: Listener mail: subject spreadsheet and Reese's email
segments.summary: Listener Robert Fiddler sent a spreadsheet grouping episodes into subjects. A listener named Reese, an eleven-year-old, wrote about a road trip to Australian Zoo and requested a voice from a past Halloween special.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address and close the show.
